extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, students, civil society and policymakers interested in the World Bank and development finance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and standards by which the World Bank's policies, governance, investments and operations are judged (environmental/social safeguards, governance, conditionality, accountability, etc.). Useful for assessing institutional performance and grant/loan practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate alignment / fossil fuel financing
rubrics_metrics.description: The World Bank should avoid financing projects that exacerbate global warming (e.g., 'A 4-degree warmer world can, and must, be avoided—we need to hold warming below 2 degrees...'). In December 2017 the Bank announced it would no longer finance fossil fuel development, but investigative reports say it continues to finance fossil fuel infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations consider whether the Bank's commitments match its lending practice (examples: activists and EU ministers calling for an end to fossil fuel funding; reports that significant trade finance was supplied to oil and gas projects in 2022). The Bank's role hosting climate funds (e.g., Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage) is also relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and social standards and monitoring (IFC/MIGA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IFC and MIGA have environmental and social standards but are criticized for relying on private-sector clients to monitor implementation and lacking independent monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics demand an extensive review of implementation strategy; assessment should check whether standards exist, how implementation is monitored, and whether independent oversight mechanisms are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance and influence (voting power and leadership selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the World Bank represents many countries, it is run by a small number of economically powerful countries; historically the president is selected from US-nominated candidates and major shareholders exert strong influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should examine voting power distribution, leadership appointment norms (e.g., presidential nomination and board confirmation for five-year terms), and whether the Bank's governance concentrates influence in a few countries and how that shapes policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of assistance conditions (conditionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue World Bank loans/aids carry unfair conditions reflecting donor interests or dominant policy doctrines (the 'Washington Consensus'), sometimes forcing policy changes with adverse social effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include imposing school fees in Ghana, water privatization in Tanzania, telecom privatization linked to disaster aid, labour 'flexibility' in Sri Lanka, and subsidy removal in Iraq. Evaluations should look at how conditions are negotiated, their social impact, and whose interests they serve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural adjustment policy impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural adjustment loans enforced policy changes (deregulation, liberalization, privatization) that in some countries led to reduced social spending, higher food prices, regression in economic growth and worsened inflation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should measure changes in social indicators, whether social spending was protected, sequencing of reforms, and whether policy reforms were appropriate to institutional capacity. The shift to Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (post-1999) is relevant context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data integrity and transparency (Doing Business scandal)
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent inquiry found World Bank leaders pressured staff to alter Doing Business data to inflate rankings for specific countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should examine data governance, independence of statistical products, mechanisms preventing manipulation, and the credibility of published indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-corruption mechanisms and internal investigation (Integrity Vice Presidency - INT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank's Integrity Vice Presidency is charged with investigating internal fraud and corruption, including complaint intake, investigation and issuing investigation reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the mandate, independence, resourcing and track record of INT (or equivalent bodies), transparency of investigations, and whether its findings lead to corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procurement practices and market effects
rubrics_metrics.description: World Bank loan agreements can force procurements of goods and services at uncompetitive, non-free-market prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should check procurement rules, competition safeguards, whether loans create distortions or lock in non-competitive suppliers, and safeguards to ensure value for money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human rights and social harm from investments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some World Bank-funded projects have been linked to severe human rights violations and social harms (examples: killings linked to a palm oil company financed by a loan, Chixoy Dam, Marlin Mine; eviction/rights violations of Maasai in Tanzania; surveillance equipment purchases in Xinjiang).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess projects for potential and actual human rights impacts, grievance mechanisms (e.g., CAO, Compliance Advisor/Ombudsman), remedial actions taken, and ex-post accountability for harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign immunity and limits on accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The World Bank requires sovereign immunity from countries it deals with, which critics say can be used as a shield to escape accountability and legal responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations should address how sovereign immunity affects the Bank's accountability, whether waivers or dispute-resolution mechanisms exist, and political dynamics (e.g., veto power of large shareholders) that limit recourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cronyism, conflicts of interest and leadership ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank has been criticized for instances of cronyism and ethical scandals (e.g., Wolfowitz pay controversy, alleged hiring favoritism and bonus awards, nepotism allegations around senior leaders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should analyze hiring practices, gift/bonus policies, nepotism/conflict-of-interest safeguards, transparency of senior management compensation and disciplinary processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of resources versus development needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite a large share of resources going to regions such as Africa (quoted ~45%), those regions still face significant financing gaps and development challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess resource allocation for alignment with needs, effectiveness of funded programs, whether prioritized sectors match country-level development priorities, and evidence of impact on financing gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on development results and monitoring outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (e.g., US Senate report) have said the Bank focuses too much on issuing loans rather than achieving concrete development results within a finite period, and have called to strengthen anti-corruption efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criteria include setting measurable outcomes, timebound targets, monitoring & evaluation systems, and whether lending is tied to demonstrable development results rather than volume of disbursed funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy appropriateness and the Washington Consensus critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank's promotion of market-oriented reforms (Washington Consensus) has been criticized for over-emphasizing GDP growth and neglecting equity, employment, and the sequencing/implementation capacity in recipient countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether policy advice considers local conditions, sequencing, distributional effects, and safeguards to prevent harm from rapid reforms; review whether emphasis on GDP growth masks weaker social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitive project design and political/cultural awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Case studies (e.g., Lesotho) show that mischaracterizing economic and political conditions and ignoring political and cultural context can lead to project failure and expansion of bureaucracy rather than poverty alleviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should judge project design on its grounding in local political economy analysis, stakeholder consultation, cultural sensitivity, and adaptability to on-the-ground realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between policy commitments and lending practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bank's public commitments (e.g., environmental pledges) have sometimes diverged from actual financing (e.g., reports of billions poured into fossil fuel projects after green pledges; pandemic bonds criticized as ineffective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether stated policies are reflected in portfolio decisions, track record of compliance with commitments, and mechanisms for aligning investment practice with policy goals.
